note.note:
Consult Summary:
- New-onset, constant, severe headache for 3 days with photophobia and visual disturbance; clinician suspects migraine and arranged in-person neurologic/ocular exam and BP check; analgesic prescribed; safety-net to ED if worsening.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Severe “blinding” headache for 3 days, impairing ability to work.
- Onset/duration/progression: Sudden onset upon awakening 3 days ago; continuous since; partially relieved by ibuprofen but never fully resolves.
- Location/character: Diffuse, worse over the right eye; occasional brief stabbing pain when standing quickly; sensation of “something moving” with sudden head movement.
- Severity: Up to 8/10, improves to ~5/10 with ibuprofen.
- Associated symptoms: Photophobia; “shooting lights”/weird visual disturbance; mild nausea without vomiting.
- Pertinent negatives: No focal neurologic symptoms (no numbness, tingling, weakness); no change in smell or taste; no fever reported; no URI/sinus symptoms, sore throat, cough, or hemoptysis; able to sleep and not woken from sleep; wakes with headache in the morning.
- Prior headaches: Intermittent, brief headaches previously responsive to ibuprofen; no prior visual symptoms, nausea, or vomiting with headaches.
- Function: Works from home; missed part/all of work over the last 3 days due to headache.
- Other: Recent optometry check reportedly showed no change in vision.

Past Medical History:
- No chronic conditions reported.
- Remote history of unspecified pain in youth; resolved; no cause identified.

Medications:
- Combined oral contraceptive pill (exact product not documented); started ~1 year ago; no side effects noted; no increase in headaches since initiation per patient.
- Ibuprofen as needed for headache (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- New prescription: A stronger NSAID “similar to ibuprofen” (dose/route/frequency not documented); advised to take with food.
- May take acetaminophen (paracetamol) concurrently (dose/route/frequency not documented).

Allergies:
- No known drug allergies.

Social History:
- Lives alone; works from home.
- Tobacco: Non-smoker.
- Alcohol: Approximately 3 drinks once weekly (patient estimate).
- Recreational drugs: Denies use.
- Travel: No recent travel abroad.

Family History:
- Mother with severe migraines associated with vomiting.
- No other family history reported.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- Examination findings: Not recorded (teleconsult).

Investigations:
- None obtained during this consult.
- Planned: In-person neurologic examination and fundoscopic (back-of-eye) evaluation; blood pressure check at visit.
- Patient-reported: Recent eye exam with no change in vision.

Assessment & Plan:
- Overall Impression:
  - New severe, continuous headache with photophobia and positive visual phenomena. Clinician impression: likely migraine-type headache; first significant episode. Given combined oral contraceptive use and persistent symptoms, in-person neurologic and ocular exam indicated to assess for secondary causes.

- DDx Integration (brief):
  - Migraine with aura (possible status migrainosus): Supported by photophobia, positive visual symptoms (“shooting lights”), unilateral peri-orbital emphasis, nausea, family history; persistent >72 hours. Opposing: first significant episode; continuous course without classic throbbing described.
  - Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST): OCP use and new persistent severe headache; some positional sensitivity. Opposing: no focal deficits, seizures, or papilledema reported.
  - Tension-type headache: Constant diffuse pain and ability to sleep are compatible. Opposing: severity, photophobia, and visual phenomena less typical.

- Issue 1:
  - Acute severe headache, likely migraine with visual aura.
  - Plan:
    - Start prescribed stronger NSAID (similar to ibuprofen); take with food. May take acetaminophen (paracetamol) concurrently. Specific dose/route/frequency not documented.
    - Schedule prompt in-person visit for full neurologic exam and fundoscopic exam.
    - Safety-net: If headache becomes unbearable, worsens, changes character (e.g., thunderclap), or if new neurologic symptoms, vomiting, fever, or neck stiffness occur, go to the emergency department.

- Issue 2:
  - Contraception in context of suspected migraine with aura.
  - Plan:
    - Check blood pressure at in-person visit.
    - If migraine with aura is confirmed, clinician advised combined OCP may not be suitable and may need to be changed. Continue current pill for now per clinician’s advice.

- Issue 3:
  - Rule-out of secondary causes (e.g., ocular or intracranial pathology).
  - Plan:
    - Perform in-person neurologic and ocular (fundoscopic) exam; management to be guided by findings.
    - Seek urgent care if red flags as above develop.

- General plan items:
  - Appointment booking via support team for in-person evaluation.
  - Patient may cancel if symptoms fully resolve before the appointment per clinician.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected: Vitals (including current BP), full neurologic exam, fundoscopic exam, detailed medication dosages/frequency, exact OCP name/strength. Temperature not measured. No imaging/labs ordered at this time.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx: None noted.
- Transcript quality: Occasional audio/clarity issues; some medication/product names redacted/not captured.
